name: Ikigai
what: A Japanese idea of what gives your life meaning and a reason to get up in the morning.
whyItMatters: It shows how many people connect daily work, family and small joys into one sense of purpose.
etiquette: Ask a local what they enjoy about their work; listen, don’t interview.
Share your own answer in return.

name: Mottainai
what: A feeling of regret when something useful is wasted, from food to time to materials.
whyItMatters: It explains the culture of repairing, reusing and wrapping things with care.
etiquette: Finish the food you order.
Carry your own bag or bottle.

name: Chanoyu (tea ceremony)
what: A ritual in which a host prepares and serves matcha to guests with mindful, practised movements.
whyItMatters: It teaches presence, respect and hospitality through a simple shared bowl of tea.
etiquette: Bow lightly to the host and say thank you.
Follow the host’s lead on how to turn and hold the bowl.
Admire the bowl after you finish.

name: Hina Matsuri
what: Girls’ Day on 3 March, when families display sets of dolls and wish for their daughters’ health.
whyItMatters: It is one of the seasonal festivals that mark the year at home.
etiquette: Look, but don’t touch the doll displays.
Ask before taking photos in a home or shop.

name: Otoshidama
what: Money given to children at New Year in small decorated envelopes.
whyItMatters: It is a family custom of good wishes for the year ahead.
etiquette: It is a family custom; visitors are not expected to give.
Receive any gift with both hands and a thank you.

name: Kimono
what: Traditional Japanese clothing, wrapped around the body and tied with an obi belt.
whyItMatters: Each style, colour and pattern can suit a season or an occasion.
etiquette: Wrap the left side over the right.
Take small steps and ask the staff if you need help sitting.

name: Bonsai
what: The art of growing a small tree in a pot and shaping it over many years.
whyItMatters: It reflects patience and respect for nature, and a bonsai is often cared for across generations.
etiquette: Don’t touch trees on display.
Ask before photographing a private collection.

name: Kintsugi
what: Repairing broken pottery with lacquer and gold so the cracks become part of the piece.
whyItMatters: It treats a break as part of an object’s story, an idea close to “repair, don’t discard”.
etiquette: Handle pieces with both hands.
Ask before photographing a maker’s work.

name: Omotenashi
what: Wholehearted hospitality, giving thought to a guest’s needs before they ask.
whyItMatters: It shapes how shops, inns and hosts welcome visitors.
etiquette: Accept kindness with a clear thank you.
Tipping is not customary in Japan.

name: Onsen etiquette
what: Bathing in natural hot-spring water, usually shared and without swimwear.
whyItMatters: It is a calm, social ritual of cleanliness and rest.
etiquette: Wash and rinse fully before entering the bath.
Keep your towel out of the water.
Ask ahead about tattoo rules.

name: Hanami
what: Gathering under blossoming cherry trees to enjoy the flowers, often with food and friends.
whyItMatters: It celebrates the short season and how quickly beautiful things pass.
etiquette: Take your rubbish home.
Don’t shake branches or climb the trees.

name: Shinto shrine manners
what: Visiting a Shinto shrine with a few simple gestures of respect.
whyItMatters: Small habits like bowing and purifying your hands show care for a shared sacred place.
etiquette: Bow lightly at the torii and walk near the edge of the path.
Rinse your hands at the water pavilion.
At the offering hall: bow twice, clap twice, bow once.

name: Buddhist temple manners
what: Visiting a Buddhist temple quietly and respectfully.
whyItMatters: Temples are places of prayer as well as sights.
etiquette: Speak softly and don’t photograph people praying.
At the hall, press your palms together; no clapping.

name: Anime and tech culture
nameJa: アニメとテクノロジー
what: Japan’s modern pop culture: anime, manga, games and electronics.
whyItMatters: It is a living art form and a major way people around the world meet Japan.
etiquette: Ask before taking photos inside shops.
Keep bags in front of you in narrow aisles.
